newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Taiwan hits all-time import/export peaks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Taiwan hits all-time import/export peaks.

text.p: Taiwan's exports and imports soared to all-time peaks in July while the trade surplus fell 59.6 percent to US$543 million, all boding well for the island's economy -- present and future -- analysts said on Thursday.

While imports rose a whopping 25.1 percent year-on-year against 13.1 percent growth for exports, analysts said the gap would narrow in coming months, reflecting the Taiwan dollar's recent fall and the annual hot sales season for electronics.
July exports totalled US$10.7 billion and imports were US$10.16 billion, both record highs for any month.
"These are very strong figures and it indicates a very bustling economy," said Nomura Securities analyst Amy Huang.
"If both the domestic and worldwide economies remain firm, exports in particular will have even more room to grow due to the Taiwan dollar's depreciation," Huang said.

The local currency in late July weakened through the T$28 level against the U.S. dollar for the first time since 1988 after the central bank dropped that defence threshold in a move widely seen as a bid to quicken Taiwan's economic lifeblood -- exports.
The local unit closed at T$28.639 on Thursday, reflecting losses of nearly four percent since July 1.
The finance ministry on Thursday predicted that second half exports would grow an annual eight percent, bringing full-1997 growth to around six percent.
The ministry said it expected even sharper import growth, forecasting a second-half rise of 11.5 percent year-on-year and 10 percent for all of 1997.

Analysts said that while a shrinking surplus may not help Taiwan's immediate economic growth, it indicated a healthy trend toward stronger local investment that will help ensure long-term evolution into a more mature economy.
"In the long run, it is not great for the economy to rely too heavily on exports," said Terry Chen, analyst for Grand Cathay Securities.

"Heavy imports may not help the economy now, but the goods coming in will boost domestic development," Chen said, noting that capital goods made up a substantial portion of Taiwan's imports and import growth.
Nomura's Huang said July's impressive trade figures attested to the strength of Taiwan's current economy.
The capitalist island posted gross domestic product growth of 6.83 percent in the first quarter and is on track to grow 6.24 percent for all of 1997, according to state projections.
Leading the economy, especially exports, in the second half will be high-technology companies, analysts say.

Blue chips like computer giant Acer Inc and microchip pioneer Taiwan Semiconductor are tipped to enjoy sizzling second-half sales due to Intel Corp's price cuts for its market-leading Pentium microprocessors.

"If Pentium prices go down, Taiwan's computer companies will see a dramatic increase in sales, which in turn will bring additional business for integrated circuit firms," said Wang Jieh, analyst for Foremost Investment Services.

Exports to Hong Kong -- the main conduit for Taiwan's lucrative trade and investment in the rival Chinese communist mainland -- should steam ahead despite Hong Kong's July 1 return to Beijing rule, analysts said.
"I can't see Hong Kong's role as the middleman changing in the foreseeable future," Grand Cathay's Chen said.
Exports to Hong Kong in July rose 20.9 percent year-on-year to US$2.54 billion, making the former British colony the second largest destination after the United States.

Taiwan, which has banned direct contacts with China since they were split by a 1949 civil war, has said it would allow businesses to continue to use Hong Kong as a trade conduit after its reabsorption by Beijing.
